how_to_use: Members of extended family and their interactions with the child (grandparents, parents). Use as starting point to talk about children’s own families, and family traditions surrounding important events like birthdays
Open discussions about sibling relationships. What can children infer about how the brothers get along from the story? Discuss different family members across generations - parents, grandparents.
Sibling relationship and mother-child relationships. Start discussions around daily routines, staying clean and good habits.
Myself/my home, and the people who share it . Trigger a writing and/or drawing activity about children’s own homes, and where certain things are kept.
Feelings and emotions associated with the first day of school. Start discussions about memories of first days at school; create empathy with the characters.
Introduces the concept of learning new things. Deals with teacher-student relationships. Specifically introduces learning second languages.
Myself, playing alone. Themes discussed include my emotions and daily routine. Reflections (science concept).
Things that make different animals unique. Start a discussion about things we have in common with others and things that make us unique.
Themes discussed include body parts - good for learning new English words. Things that we have in common; things that make us special. Pets and animals
My five senses and how they are used. Discussion of different body parts and what they are used for.
Reasons for feelings sad; how to feel better. Friendship and helping others .
Discusses different emotions. Talk about emotions shown in the pictures. How can you tell how the characters are feeling? What is making each of them feel that way?
Start a discussion about what happens when we have a difference of opinion to our friends. Talk about listening to others, other points of view, kindness

Start a discussion about different types of friends. Talk about the different things (play games, talk, teach things, read, listen etc) we do with our friends. Overlap between friends and family. Talk about what makes a good friend.
Talk about making friends, importance of friendship. Why might you be sad if you didn’t have any friends?
Talk about pets as part of the family. Start a discussion about the different kind of pets you could or do have. Talk about telling stories from different perspectives
Discuss pet animals and characteristics of a cat.
Animal story featuring fawn, elephant, monkey, bear. Can also use to talk about kindness, friendship and family.
Animal story. Discussions of what makes a friendship. Humorous story to read aloud.
Characteristics of different animals, including a turtle; a cheetah; a whale; a canary; an elephant; a frog; a bee; a dinosaur.
Different animals and the noises they make - good for reading aloud and encouraging children to guess noises/join in.
Characteristics of a cat (pet animals).Read the story aloud and ask children to recall what characteristics/traits a cat has.

Read the story aloud and ask children to recall what characteristics/traits an owl has. Ask children to come up with a ‘day in the life’ of another animal in groups verbally, or as a written exercise alone
Discussion of what characteristics a monkey has. How are the boy and the monkey similar? How are they different? What other characteristics that you have can you compare to animals? Why
Read the story aloud and ask children to recall what characteristics/traits ants have.
Read the story aloud and ask children to recall what characteristics/traits ants have.
Read the story aloud and ask children to recall what characteristics/traits crows have. Where do they live? What do they eat? What do they like to do? Talk about the noises animals make.

Use the book to encourage children to identify birds they see around them. Ask children to describe (either verbally or in writing) each bird, using the images. Ask them to think about colours, shapes, size, and other features.

Presented as a riddle, so can use as an inference/prediction exercise. Stop reading at certain points and ask children to guess. Stop and explain specific words that have certain meanings when associated with a river e.g. ‘mouth’ - give children examples from their specific context.This should perhaps be Level 2?
Has different seasons within one book, so can be used to introduce the concept of season, as well as to talk about sequence and time.

Use to talk about different seasons, ask children about their favourite seasons, and why that is. Could talk about what different types of clothing are suitable for different types of weather and why. Introduce the difference between ‘weather’ and ‘season’. Talk about rhyming words - ask children to find rhyming words in the text.
Use to support the activities above. Note that this is a community story and there are some issues with grammar/punctuation.
Use to talk about spring season. Ask children about their favourite seasons, and why that is. Ask children to recall all the different things the girl does and sees in spring.

Talk about the different types of food grown in the book. What colour are they? How do they grow? What are the different ways in which we can eat them? Ask children to think of more foods that grow in the ground/from the ground/on trees/on bushes etc.
Introduce the different food ‘groups’. Talk about foods children like and don’t like.Talk about the flavours (sweet; sour; savoury etc) of the foods in the story.
Talk about Pongal and spring festivals . Art - talk about different places and ways of drawing. Introduce constellations.
Introduces Diwali. Talk about other festivals which are celebrated in the winter season.
Talk about (Hindu) festivals. Ask children to think of more festivals which are celebrated in India.

Start a conversation about different modes of transport. When might you travel by train/car/bus/cycle/bike/auto/boat etc. Why? What are the advantages and disadvantages of different modes of transport?

Start a conversation about different modes of transport. When might you travel by train/car/bus/cycle/bike/auto/boat etc. Why? What are the advantages and disadvantages of different modes of transport?
A number of simple opposites are given (one per page), so you can use this to introduce the concept of opposites very clearly, before moving on to the other stories.
Give children ‘half’ of each opposite pair and ask children to find the other in the story. Why do they think that the king has become thin?

Use the activity at the end of the book. Pause when you are reading the story and ask children to think of opposite words (e.g you could stop at words like: faster, noisy, danger; love; strong, shut).
Ask children to think of more objects which are curly and straight
Talk about the different colours in the story (the raincoat is red, the sky is blue, the sun is yellow). Introduce the concept of primary colours and how they can be mixed to make tertiary colours.
Introduce the concept of primary colours and how they can be mixed to make tertiary colours.Talk about the different words for colours in other languages the children may know.
Talk about imagination, and drawing things according to your imagination. Start an art activity in which the children mix and match colours to make unusual animals.
Basic introduction to colours

Activity based on different shades of the same colour, inspired by the shades on each page. Vocabulary expansion: talk about words to describe colours more specifically (e.g. midnight blue; navy blue; saffron; magenta etc). Ask children to think of more objects in the colour given on each page as you are reading it.
Introduce the concept of verbs. Pick out and discuss specific verbs in the story: racing; leapt; ran; stumbled etc.
Adjectives. Also talk about similes e.g. ‘round as a drum’ ‘like a ball of cotton’. Talk about the difference between similes and metaphors.
Introduce prepositions. Talk about opposite words for the prepositions in the book.
Introduce prepositions. Talk about opposite words for the prepositions in the book.
Letter ‘y’ phonics sound. Prepositions - talk about each preposition and its opposite. Also good habits (sharing).
Use for a phonics lesson - Ch sound, D sound, Sh sound, Cr sound.Identify rhyming words
Use for a phonics lesson - Ch sound.
Use for a phonics lesson (a). Can also talk about the verbs in the story.
Phonics (letter ‘s’) - all the names which begin with ‘s’. Ask children to guess the name of the main character before she reveals what her name is.
Phonics (letter ‘b’ for banana)
Phonics (S for slurp and B for burp). Rhyming words - ask children to identify the words that rhyme .
Rhyming words and verbs - can ask children to identify examples of both within the story. Also examples of similes. Why do we use similes? What sort of pictures do they help create in our minds?
Rhyming words. Phonics (Th for thup, H for Ha, Y for Yum etc).
English language: correct use of apostrophes, lots of clear examples of using verbs
What good habits can children identify in the book? For example: tidying up, being helpful, working together.
What good habits can children identify in the book? For example: being helpful, being creative, thinking of solutions, saying thank you, fixing things, recycling, helping elders

What bad habits can children identify in the book? For example: doing things which your parents have said ‘no’ to, being rude; not asking nicely; being grumpy. What good habits do the puppies bring out in Anil?
What good habits can children identify in the book? For example: helping your parents, being kind to your siblings, taking care of those younger than you, helping with chores, reading books

What good habits can children identify in the book? For example: waking up early, brushing your teeth, having breakfast, staying clean. What bad habits can children identify in the book? For example: not waking up on time, being grumpy.

Introduce concepts of good dental hygiene, brushing your teeth twice daily after eating food. Talk about foods which are good for your teeth and foods which are bad for your teeth (e.g. too much sugar).

Introduce concepts of good dental hygiene, brushing your teeth twice daily after eating food. Talk about foods which are good for your teeth and foods which are bad for your teeth (e.g. too much sugar).

Introduce concepts of staying clean, taking a bath on a daily basis. Can also angle from a science perspective and introduce bacteria/germs. Can do a practical demonstration of how to effectively wash your hands.
Life skills - importance of hard work, perseverance
Talk about different ‘lines’ - curly, straight, jagged, diagonal, wavy. Ask children to draw each, and find examples of all of them in the environment around them
Various science concepts: how does a magnifying glass work? (lesson on lenses); how do magnets work? (could be a practical lesson with magnets).
Concept of day and night, sun and moon.
Talk about shapes - 3D and 2D shapes. Identify circles and spheres in the environment around you.

Big and small, and sequences. Give children examples of different sized objects and ask them to place them in order. Introduce concept that big and small is relative to other things. E.g. a dog might be ‘big’ until a bigger dog comes along. Also introduction of superlatives e.g. big bigger biggest.
Maths: practical way to introduce the concept of zero . How can there be nothing? Can illustrate with objects
Can be used for Counting (see page 5) . Talk about the concepts of ‘less’ ‘more’ ‘many and ‘few’.
Talking points for this particular book include: birthdays, gifts, helping others, having empathy, family roles, new siblings, feeling sad and then feeling better
Talking points for this particular book include: imagination, colours, helping others, making friends
Talking points for this particular book include: growing food, weather, imagination.
Good for engaging children because: it has lots of action and a clear sequence of events.
Good for engaging children because: it’s funny!
Good for engaging children because: they can guess what is happening at various points in the story.
Good for engaging children because: allows you to talk about imagination, creative thinking, dreaming
Points to think about: Have children thought about their room/mother/fears when visualizing the story? Can they relate to the situation and share some examples from their own experience?
Have they ever been to the zoo? Which parts of the story require you to especially use your imagination? Why?
Have they ever been to the zoo? Which parts of the story require you to especially use your imagination? Why?
Do the characters in the book remind you of anyone you know?
Have you ever watched ants at work? What did you observe?
Points to think about: What season is Manu waiting for? Do you enjoy the rainy season? What’s good about it? What’s not so good?
Points to think about:Without much description from the text, how did you make the picture of the king and the dog more detailed in your mind?
How easy/hard was it to picture an animal that you have never seen before? Which parts of the story helped you picture Munia?

Points to think about: Which parts of the story were realistic? Which were less realistic? What helped you to imagine the less realistic parts? How can metaphors and similes help us to visualize? (see page 4)
Discussion about their memories of their first day at school
Pointers: Do they remember being told that they have to wait for something? What?; What has made them feel angry in the past? Why?; Do they have memories of their own birthdays?
Pointers: has anyone had an imaginary friend?
Pointers: has anyone had an imaginary friend?
